title: A reading after death
hook: a complete reading of the Granth follows a death, often over days
tomorrow: the last page is read. is the final prayer for him, or for us?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashes to running water: return to water, the father, any river that keeps moving. Back from the river, the family goes to the gurdwara.

When someone dies, you'd expect a special reading: a funeral text, chosen for grief. So here's the odd thing. The reading that Sikhs begin after a death opens on the same page as every reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, Ang 1, and goes on to the very end, through every hymn in between. On the gurdwara wall there's a sign-up sheet with Baba Kartar's name at the top and empty slots below it. Simran writes her own name in one of them, then stares at it, because her Gurmukhi is slow.
screen: `NOT A FUNERAL TEXT.` → `THE SAME FIRST PAGE AS EVERY READING.` → `A SIGN-UP SHEET ON THE WALL.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, says that after a death a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or at a gurdwara, and the family and sangat join in. Often it's a sehaj path: a complete reading at an unhurried pace, taken in turns over days. So why the whole book, starting at the beginning? Here's the answer to the puzzle. The comfort isn't kept in one chapter for sad occasions. It's the whole Guru. Over those days the family hears praise and longing, wedding songs and laments, the Gurus and the bhagats, morning prayers and night ones: all of a life, read for one life. And here's something to tell a friend tonight: the reading after a death opens on the same first page as every reading of the Granth. Nothing is skipped because the occasion is sad. On Thursday at seven, Simran sits on the cushion behind the Granth, a granthi beside her for help. She reads her stretch slowly, stumbles on a long word, starts it again. Nobody minds. That's what sehaj means: unhurried.
screen: `THE CODE: BEGIN A READING.` · `SEHAJ PATH: UNHURRIED, IN TURNS.` · `THE WHOLE GURU, NOT ONE CHAPTER.` · `SIMRAN'S STRETCH, SLOWLY.` · then, large: `READ FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Open any page of Gurbani you have: a gutka, a book, a shabad on your phone. Read a few lines aloud, slowly, for someone you've lost or someone who is struggling. If the words are hard, say them anyway; stumbling counts.
A reading after death. Sikhs begin a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, often a sehaj path, taken in turns over days.
Hold onto this: read for them, every page, at whatever speed you have. Thursday, seven o'clock, done.

sehaj path.meaning: a complete, unhurried reading of the Granth, in turns

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's morning prayer, the opening of the Granth

bhagats.meaning: saint-poets, not Gurus, whose hymns are in the Granth

granthi.meaning: a person who reads and cares for the Granth

Gurmukhi.meaning: the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in
